Title: Fine grain algorithm parallelization on a hybrid control-flow and dataflow processor
Text:
Fine grain algorithm parallelization 
on a hybrid control‑flow and dataflow processor
Nenad Korolija1*

Abstract 
The execution time of a high-performance computing algorithm is influenced by vari-
ous factors, including the algorithm’s scalability, the selected hardware for processing 
elements, and the communication speed between these elements. This study utilizes 
a hybrid architecture that integrates both control-flow and dataflow hardware. Specifi-
cally, the control-flow hardware encompasses both multicore and manycore architec-
tures. Guidance for dataflow programmers is provided to enable them to anticipate 
the level of acceleration achievable with a hybrid control-flow and dataflow architec-
ture before developing dataflow hardware algorithms. Furthermore, the methodology 
developed is introduced, offering a structured approach for programmers to decom-
pose algorithms and optimize each segment by leveraging the most suitable archi-
tectural type. The prerequisite for a programmer is not to know hardware description 
languages, but he must be well-versed in estimating the complexity of an algorithm. 
This study represents the culmination of over a decade of expertise in hybrid control-
flow and dataflow architectures. It provides a detailed methodology for decomposing 
a control-flow algorithm into segments optimized for dataflow architectures and those 
better suited to control-flow architectures. The Lattice-Boltzmann method is employed 
as a representative example, implemented on both control-flow and dataflow hard-
ware. The estimated total acceleration factor of the decomposed Lattice-Boltzmann 
method on the hybrid architecture, relative to execution times using control-flow 
and dataflow hardware, is approximately two for a given matrix dimension. The find-
ings underscore the advantages of employing a hybrid architecture, demonstrating 
significant acceleration potential even for algorithms traditionally optimized for data-
flow architectures. The primary benefit of the hybrid architecture lies in its capac-
ity to accelerate algorithms where only specific portions are suitable for dataflow 
hardware.
Keywords:  Control-flow architectures, Dataflow architectures, Hybrid architectures, 
Algorithm parallelization

This section will first outline the fundamental principles of control-flow and dataflow 
computing paradigms, followed by a comparative analysis of these paradigms. This com-
parison will provide a methodology for algorithm decomposition, guiding the determi-
nation of each segment’s suitability for either control-flow or dataflow architectures [2].
When programming dataflow architectures, certain segments of an algorithm may 
not be well-suited for dataflow execution and thus need to be processed on control-flow 
architectures. Repeatedly transferring data between these architectures during algo-
rithm execution can impact the overall execution time due to communication delays. A 
potential solution to this issue may be identified through a thorough review of the exist-
ing literature in this domain.
Control‑flow paradigm basics
The control-flow paradigm is rooted in the principles established by the von Neumann 
architecture. Initially, this paradigm is exemplified by single-core processors, which have 
since evolved into multi-core and manycore processors.
Control-flow computer architecture operates by transferring a program from disk to 
main memory, where it is subsequently processed. The execution of instructions within 
this paradigm can be delineated into several distinct phases: instruction fetch, operation 
decoding, operand retrieval, execution of the operation on the operands, result storage, 
and interrupt handling. Prior to the execution of an instruction, it must first be loaded 
into the instruction register (IR). According to the von Neumann architecture, the pro-
gram counter (PC) register contains the address of the next instruction to be executed 
and is incremented after each instruction fetch from memory.
Once an instruction is fetched into the instruction register (IR), its operation code 
(opcode) is extracted and decoded. Based on the decoded opcode, the processor deter-
mines the sources of the operands. Some operands may be readily available within the 
processor (e.g., in the IR or other registers), while others need to be retrieved from main 
memory. Following operand preparation, the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) performs the 
operation, after which the result is stored. During the storage phase, the ALU’s output 
is transferred to the appropriate register or written to main memory. Additionally, if 
an interrupt occurs during instruction execution, it must be evaluated for acceptance. 
Rejection of the interrupt may occur due to reasons such as a higher or equal priority 
of the currently executing code, or a disabled interrupt bit in the program status word. 
If the interrupt is accepted, the current execution context is saved on the stack to ena-
ble restoration after the interrupt handling routine is completed. Figure 1 illustrates the 
control-flow architecture and highlights the drawbacks associated with the necessity of 
communication between the processor and memory for each operand not held in the 
cache.
One of the advantages of the control-flow paradigm is its ability to execute instruc-
tions in any sequence specified by the program. This inherent flexibility renders con-
trol-flow architecture highly adaptable and effective for executing a wide range of

programs in which the execution of the same set of instructions does not repeat many 
times so it would be beneficial to parallelize it using multiple processors.
A significant drawback of the control-flow paradigm is the complexity of its con-
trol logic, which results in substantial consumption of chip die area. This complexity 
not only reduces the number of transistors available for instruction processing but 
also leads to excessive bus utilization as data must be repeatedly transmitted. For 
instance, if multiple instructions depend on the result of a single prior instruction, 
each dependent instruction must repeatedly access the same data via the bus.
Multicore and manycore architectures, which are built upon the control-flow par-
adigm, address this issue by employing multiple cores that operate under the same 
principles but execute in parallel. These cores share the same cache memory and 
RAM, facilitating faster processing due to improved communication speed between 
cores. However, despite these advancements, the fundamental bottlenecks associated 
with control-flow architectures persist.
Dataflow paradigm basics
Dataflow can be categorized into software and hardware types. Software dataflow 
operates within control-flow architectures that implement dataflow principles, such 
as superscalar processors, which utilize multiple cores to execute instructions from 
a ready queue as they become available. This study focuses specifically on hardware 
dataflow architectures [3].
The dataflow paradigm is predicated on the principle of data propagation through 
computational hardware. This concept, while historically rooted, continues to be piv-
otal in modern computing architectures. Notably, Honeycomb architectures exem-
plify the application of dataflow principles [4]. Contemporary hardware designs can 
either be purpose-built, such as application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), or 
adaptable, typically implemented via field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). This 
discussion will center on reconfigurable dataflow architectures, presenting a cohesive 
overview of the paradigm. Initially, foundational concepts will be introduced, fol-
lowed by a critical examination of both advantages and limitations. Some nuanced 
aspects of the dataflow paradigm may not be addressed immediately, as the discussion 
assumes familiarity with control-flow architectures. Comparative analysis between 
dataflow and control-flow paradigms will be employed to elucidate key distinctions.

In dataflow hardware, the execution of instructions can be analogized to a manufac-
turing process using conveyor belts. In this paradigm, the hardware is designed to per-
form a specific set of operations, with data moving through the system as a consequence 
of voltage differentials between input and output points. A discrete unit within this 
hardware that executes a single operation is referred to as a processing element. Unlike 
control-flow architectures, where bus congestion can be a limiting factor, dataflow archi-
tectures mitigate this issue since result data propagates directly from one processing ele-
ment to another as needed. Additionally, dataflow hardware systems may incorporate 
memory chips. As illustrated in Fig. 2, a key characteristic of dataflow architectures is 
their operational frequency, which is typically an order of magnitude lower than that of 
control-flow architectures. Consequently, dataflow systems tend to consume less power 
per instruction executed.
A significant advantage of the dataflow paradigm is its facilitation of implicit paral-
lel processing. Since each processing element executes a single operation, the theoreti-
cal upper limit for the number of instructions that can be executed in parallel within 
a dataflow architecture is constrained by the number of processing elements available. 
This number can potentially reach into the thousands, contingent upon the resource 
requirements for individual instructions and the forwarding of results. For instance, if 
an arithmetic operation on a single bit requires only a few transistors, a 64-bit arithmetic 
operation could be achieved with fewer than 1000 transistors. Therefore, a billion tran-
sistors could theoretically support up to one million processing elements.
In dataflow architectures, data propagation between processing elements eliminates 
the need for a central bus, which often serves as a bottleneck in control-flow architec-
tures. Moreover, the use of field-programmable gate arrays in dataflow systems typically 
limits operational frequencies to approximately an order of magnitude lower than those 
achievable with control-flow architectures. This reduced frequency contributes to signif-
icantly lower power consumption per instruction executed when compared to control-
flow architectures.
A notable drawback of the dataflow paradigm is its typically lower clock frequency 
compared to control-flow processors. This reduction in clock frequency can impact 
overall performance. Additionally, dataflow architectures based on field-programma-
ble gate arrays necessitate reconfiguration before an algorithm can be executed. This 
reconfiguration process can be time-consuming, with the preparation of the FPGA

However, in many cases, the usage profile and iteration count are not known a priori. 
Furthermore, dataflow architectures are predominantly suited for high-performance

Figure 3 illustrates a hybrid processor architecture that integrates both control-flow 
and dataflow processing units on a single chip die. This processor configuration features 
direct connectivity between the control-flow and dataflow hardware, cache memories, 
and the internal bus. The inclusion of hierarchical cache memories facilitates concur-
rent operation of the dataflow hardware alongside multicore and manycore architec-
tures, enabling efficient data sharing and coordination between the different processing 
units. This hybrid approach leverages the strengths of both paradigms to optimize per-
formance and flexibility in computational tasks.
This work centers on the algorithm decomposition methodology, designed to partition 
algorithms such that specific segments can be executed using control-flow architectures 
(such as multicore and manycore processors), while other segments are executed on 
dataflow hardware. The approach outlined in this manuscript is intended to be broadly 
applicable. Consequently, the architectural comparisons provided are presented in a 
general context, avoiding hardware-specific details wherever feasible.
The subsequent section outlines the problem definition and is followed by a review of 
relevant literature. The section on the proposed solution begins with an evaluation of 
the suitability of control-flow and dataflow hardware for executing specific instructions. 
This analysis will inform the categorization of high-performance computing algorithms 
based on their execution profiles. Algorithms will be examined in terms of their paral-
lelism—some featuring many independent instructions capable of concurrent execution, 
while others may involve dependent iterations but operate on large datasets.
Following this categorization, the two computing paradigms will be assessed in 
relation to the identified types of algorithms. The subsequent section addresses the 
challenge of integrating substantially different computer architectures for executing

Problem definition
The challenge of accelerating high-performance computing algorithms, particu-
larly those involved in processing large datasets [6], represents a fundamental issue 
in computer science. The significance of this challenge is underscored by its critical 
applications across various domains, including physics, technology, and engineering. 
Common strategies for enhancing the performance of these algorithms include opti-
mizing the algorithms themselves, selecting the most appropriate computing archi-
tectures, and modifying the execution flow to better leverage hardware capabilities. 
These approaches aim to maximize computational efficiency and effectiveness in han-
dling complex and data-intensive tasks.
This work is predicated on the integration of control-flow and dataflow paradigms 
within a single chip architecture. The control-flow paradigm underpins both multi-
core processors and manycore architectures, such as those found in modern graph-
ics processing units (GPUs). The primary objective is to enhance the performance of 
high-performance algorithms by leveraging the strengths of each paradigm accord-
ing to their respective suitability. Specifically, the approach aims to optimize com-
putational efficiency by strategically utilizing control-flow mechanisms for tasks 
well-suited to them and dataflow mechanisms for tasks that benefit from parallel data 
processing.
The objective of this research is to decompose existing algorithms, which are at 
least partially amenable to execution on dataflow hardware, into segments that are 
tailored for execution on different architectural paradigms. Many of the algorithms 
contain portions that are not suitable for dataflow architectures, such as the initiali-
zation of data for processing or finalizing the execution of the algorithm and storing 
data. The communication cost between two types of hardware in this scenario can 
often be neglected compared to the execution time. This comes from the fact that 
the time needed for processing elements should overpass the time needed for the 
communication between two types of hardware, while otherwise it would not be jus-
tifiable to send data from control-flow to dataflow hardware and, optionally, return 
results. However, if the computationally demanding portion of the algorithm that is 
responsible for almost all of the total execution time of the algorithm has portions 
suitable for different architectures, frequent communication between two types of 
hardware can jeopardize the acceleration possibilities using the dataflow hardware.
Another goal of this research is to find suitable architecture for executing algo-
rithms that require frequent communication between control-flow and dataflow 
hardware. Further, a fine-grain algorithm analysis is essential, wherein the individual 
segments of the algorithm are evaluated in relation to the underlying hardware.

Existing solutions
This section will present solutions to the problem of accelerating high-performance 
computing algorithms from both control-flow and dataflow perspectives. Subse-
quently, it will introduce a hybrid model that integrates control-flow and dataflow 
hardware within a single chip die. This approach aims to leverage the advantages of 
both paradigms to optimize performance and efficiency in computational tasks.
The optimal solution identified within the realm of control-flow computing involves 
the deployment of thousands of processors on a single chip die. These architectures, 
commonly found in graphics processing units (GPUs), can be adapted for high-per-
formance computing algorithms. Despite their capacity to execute instructions in an 
arbitrary order, these architectures are still constrained by inherent bottlenecks in 
control-flow hardware, which limits the extent of parallelization achievable.
The most effective solution identified within the domain of dataflow computing 
involves accelerating algorithms using a configuration where control-flow processors 
and dataflow hardware are physically separated. While this architecture supports uni-
form processing, it often encounters bottlenecks related to the communication speed 
between the disparate components, particularly during data initialization or when 
handling edge cases that necessitate distinct processing approaches.
To illustrate the application of the proposed method, consider the Lattice-Boltz-
mann method as an example algorithm. The best result found in the open literature is 
presented in the study "Accelerating the Lattice-Boltzmann Method Using the Max-
eler Dataflow Approach" [7]. In this study, the authors implemented a dataflow ver-
sion of the Lattice-Boltzmann method, achieving an acceleration factor of 110 and 
demonstrating a notable reduction in energy consumption.
One of the main gaps in executing high-performance computing algorithms with 
dataflow hardware arises from the fact that certain processing tasks are inherently 
more suited to control-flow hardware. Concurrently, the communication speed 
between control-flow and dataflow architectures imposes limitations on the poten-
tial for parallelization. This restriction hampers the ability to distribute an algorithm’s 
execution across both architectures, with some portions running on dataflow hard-
ware and others on control-flow hardware. The resulting communication bottlenecks 
between these disparate processing units can undermine the efficiency of such hybrid 
execution strategies.
Researchers have developed prototypes of hybrid processors that integrate both con-
trol-flow and dataflow hardware on the same chip [8, 9]. This architecture facilitates 
the execution of both control-flow and dataflow algorithms, thereby enhancing the 
efficiency of cluster and cloud infrastructures. The control-flow hardware component 
includes both multicore and manycore processors. Communication between these com-
ponents is managed through shared cache memories [10], which aim to accelerate access 
to shared data and allow multiple processors to utilize the same data without requiring 
complex inter-processor communication.
The hybrid architecture detailed in [11] bears resemblance to the previously men-
tioned designs but lacks explicit guidelines for its utilization. Additionally, researchers 
have addressed the limitations of register files in processors by reorganizing data flow to 
enable direct communication between processing units, thereby mitigating register file

bottlenecks [12]. Despite resolving some bottleneck issues, challenges associated with 
control-flow architectures persist.
Further research has focused on mapping high-performance scientific comput-
ing algorithms onto superscalar processors to minimize data thrashing, where data is 
repeatedly sent to and from any type of resource that can potentially become the bot-
tleneck [13]. These architectures are often referred to as software dataflow architectures. 
The approach to avoiding bottlenecks in these architectures parallels the Maxeler frame-
work’s methodology for hardware dataflow architectures based on FPGAs.
Moreover, some researchers have proposed hybrid architectures that integrate con-
trol-flow and dataflow processing with Internet of Things (IoT) capabilities on the same 
chip die, known as the Ultimate Dataflow [14]. This architecture aims to address the 
increasing demands of the IoT.
The integration of advantageous features from multiple computer architectures on a 
single chip die can be viewed as a form of implantation, wherein established concepts 
are applied in a novel context to achieve superior results compared to prior solutions 
[15]. The primary advantage of such a combined architecture is that it enables commu-
nication between control-flow and dataflow hardware via shared cache memories. This 
configuration reduces the distance data must travel, thereby enhancing the speed of 
communication and overall performance [16].
Weng et al. [17] have addressed specific problems of using digital signal processors 
that are of interest for many applications, including 5G networking. They categorize spa-
tial architectures in two dimensions, based on scheduling and resability of processing 
elements (PEs) on: (1) static or dynamic scheduling, and (2) dedicated or shared PEs. 
The first one is determined based on whether the timing of all instructions can be deter-
mined statically. The second one distinguishes whether each PE is dedicated to a single 
ation or shared among multiple instructions. Their proposed Revel architecture achieves 
an acceleration factor of 37 compared to DSPs. A similar approach from Weng et al. [18] 
proposes coarse-grained reconfigurable dataflow processor that enables extensive shar-
ing of computing and storage resources. The proposed dataflow processor is suitable 
for neural network and for timing sequence-dependent applications, such as video con-
text understanding and language processing. Their architecture employs a hierarchical 
design methodology, including PEs, hardware thread, and system-on-chip. Both archi-
tectures exhibit performance improvements, but they are designed and limited for a spe-
cific types of algorithms that have certain properties, e.g. for loops with variable sizes. 
A typical example application could be modeling structures for simulating earthquakes 
[19].
Proposed solution
This section is structured into three distinct parts. The first part delineates the differ-
ences between control-flow and dataflow computing, focusing on aspects such as pro-
cessing mechanisms, speed, and power consumption. The second part categorizes 
high-performance computing algorithms according to the types of processing they 
require. The final part presents a methodology for decomposing algorithms into seg-
ments that are optimized for execution on various hardware architectures.

Determining the suitability of control‑flow and dataflow hardware for specific instructions
This section offers a broad comparison of control-flow and dataflow architectures, 
examining their processing capabilities, constraints, and power consumption character-
istics. This comparison aims to establish fundamental guidelines for identifying which 
segments of high-performance computing algorithms are best suited for each type of 
architecture.
The most distinguishing characteristic of control-flow architecture is its ability to exe-
cute any instruction defined by the architecture. Enhancements in these architectures 
typically focus on increasing the number of cores. Consequently, acceleration in algo-
rithm execution within control-flow architectures is contingent upon the algorithm’s 
scalability.
Dataflow processing can be analogized to a manufacturing process where data is 
treated as a semi-finished product moving along conveyor belts. This paradigm is par-
ticularly well-suited for parallelizing loops in high-performance computing algorithms 
that account for the majority of computational time. The primary constraint of dataflow 
processing is that iterations must be independent; however, if iterations are not inher-
ently independent, the algorithm reorganization may achieve the independence among 
iterations.
Table 1 outlines the general acceleration potential of control-flow and dataflow archi-
tectures. In this table, a minus sign (−) indicates that utilizing the architecture for the 
specified problem is not advisable. A single plus sign ( +) denotes that the architec-
ture can handle the problem, albeit with suboptimal performance. A double plus sign 
(+ +) signifies that the architecture can execute the algorithm more efficiently, while a 
triple plus sign (+ + +) indicates that the architecture is specifically optimized for that 
particular type of problem. This notation will be consistently applied throughout the 
manuscript.
Non-scalable algorithms do not fully exploit parallel processing capabilities. However, 
this limitation can be mitigated by identifying and isolating portions of the algorithm 
that can be executed in parallel. By doing so, a multicore processor can still achieve 
acceleration, although the improvement may not reach the magnitude of two or more 
orders of magnitude. The extent of parallel processing benefits is influenced by the num-
ber of cores in control-flow architectures or the available resources (such as memory and 
FPGAs) in dataflow architectures. The table presented is intended to be general and is 
not specific to any particular architecture or algorithm.
Not all algorithms exhibit scalability. This discussion encompasses not only high-
performance algorithms but also more general classes of algorithms, recognizing that 
high-performance algorithms may include subcomponents that do not themselves meet 
high-performance criteria. Consequently, a non-scalable algorithm is often unsuitable 
for manycore architectures, as it may result in the underutilization of the majority of the

cores. Similarly, the dataflow paradigm is also inadequate for such algorithms. Table 2 
delineates the constraints imposed by multicore, manycore, and dataflow architectures 
on different types of instruction execution patterns. The characteristics listed in the 
table are defined as follows:
–	 Dependent iterations—Many high-performance computing algorithms incorpo-
rate loops that are iterated repeatedly. In certain scenarios, these iterations can be 
executed concurrently, as they are independent of one another. Conversely, there are 
cases where the execution of an iteration is contingent upon the result of the preced-
ing iteration, leading to dependencies between iterations. We can classify these itera-
tions as independent in the former case and dependent in the latter.
–	 Variable instructions—Simulating elementary volumes typically necessitates uniform 
processing across each volume. This uniformity facilitates straightforward paralleli-
zation of such algorithms across various discussed architectures. In contrast, data 
mining algorithms that dynamically select execution paths based on specific data 
may execute different instructions during each iteration. This variability complicates 
the definition of a consistent execution pattern within a limited set of instructions or 
program statements. Consequently, for these algorithms, it is appropriate to consider 
them as high-performance algorithms with a variable instruction set per iteration.
Compared to manycore and dataflow architectures, multicore architectures generally 
execute a smaller number of instructions per second, which limits their suitability for 
high-performance computing applications. Manycore architectures leverage the advan-
tages of control-flow processing over dataflow processing, making them well-suited 
for high-performance computing algorithms characterized by dependent consecutive 
loop iterations and complex conditional branches where execution paths cannot be 
determined at compile time. In contrast, some of these constraints may be mitigated if 
algorithms are adapted for dataflow architectures, which are designed to handle highly 
parallelizable tasks with predictable execution patterns.
High-performance computing architectures can consume power on a scale several 
orders of magnitude greater than that of personal computers. Power consumption per 
instruction can be defined as the amount of electrical power expended by the architec-
ture for executing a single instruction. This metric is crucial in evaluating the efficiency 
of high-performance systems. When multiple instructions are executed in parallel, the 
overall power consumption of the hardware can be apportioned among the individual 
instructions. This means that a specific portion of the total power consumption can be 
attributed to each instruction, reflecting its contribution to the overall energy expendi-
ture during parallel execution. Table  3 provides a comparative analysis of multicore,

the dataflow paradigm as the most power-efficient architecture currently available.
High‑performance computing algorithm categorization
The objective of this section is to delineate the general characteristics of various algo-
rithm types and their implications for execution on control-flow versus dataflow archi-
tectures. By identifying and analyzing the execution patterns inherent to algorithms of 
these types, it will be feasible to decompose them into segments that are optimally suited 
for either control-flow or dataflow architectures. This analysis aims to facilitate the effec-
tive mapping of algorithms to the most appropriate architectural paradigms based on 
their execution characteristics.
Matrix and vector processing are among the most prevalent forms of computation in 
high-performance computing. Numerous simulations in physics involve partitioning a 
three-dimensional simulation volume into elementary volumes and applying uniform 
processing to each volume, with the exception of boundary volumes, commonly referred 
to as edge cases. Additionally, theoretical physics often leverages simulations in higher-
dimensional spaces, as discussed in [20], to explore complex phenomena and theoretical 
models.
In certain simulations, each elementary volume may have multiple potential pro-
cessing paths contingent upon specific conditions. For instance, in the simulation of 
molecular reactions [21], the execution path may vary based on factors such as user 
input, the distance between molecules, the presence of larger molecular complexes, 
and the feasibility of complex movement or adjustments required within the simula-
tion volume. Similarly, in neural network simulations [22], a diverse array of execu-
tion patterns may arise, making it challenging to predict which portions of the code

Some simulations do have a predetermined number of iterations, whereas some 
assume iterating towards a result, where the iteration count is not known in advance, 
but it depends on the state of the simulation. Often, the simulation is considered to be 
finished when the estimated simulation error becomes acceptable, or the difference 
of the system state between two consecutive iterations becomes neglectable. In some 
cases, the execution pattern might depend on the human controlling the simulation, 
as is the medicine case [23].
Data mining algorithms frequently exhibit dependent execution flows, where the 
paths taken during source code execution can be influenced by multiple factors. 
These factors may include data recently read from memory or simulation results that 
necessitate a transition to alternative processing methods [24]. Such dependencies 
can result in dynamically changing execution paths, requiring adaptive processing 
strategies to handle the variability in algorithmic behavior.

architectures for processing both scalable and non-scalable algorithms, and Table 2 
offers detailed insights based on the instruction sets executed per iteration, Table 4 
specifically addresses the potential for dataflow acceleration when handling various 
portions of algorithms. This table considers algorithms with loops and a relatively

The parallel processing execution patterns can be defined based on the amount of data 
they operate with and the repeatability of instructions:
–	 Repeating a few dependent instructions, not data—this corresponds to relatively 
short loop iterations, usually not worth parallelizing.
–	 Repeating many dependent instructions, not data—this corresponds to the consider-
able portion of the algorithm belonging to a single loop, and each iteration depends 
on the previous one, making it suitable for execution on the dataflow architecture, 
optionally with re-orchestrating the execution of iterations.
–	 Repeating independent instructions, not data—this corresponds to highly scalable 
algorithms.
–	 Big data, low processing—this corresponds to accessing the big data with not much 
processing per each byte on average.
–	 Big data, repeating instructions—this corresponds to a high-performance computing 
algorithm that works with big data.
–	 Big data, non-uniform instructions—this corresponds to the process of reading big 
data, while the processing of the data is not uniform, since it depends on the data 
itself. Therefore, many big data applications might not be suitable for dataflow pro-
cessing, unless the processing can be re-orchestrated [25].
In scenarios involving the repetition of a limited number of dependent instructions 
(with minimal data access), the computational workload is insufficient to justify the 
overhead associated with communication, data initialization, and finalization for either 
manycore or dataflow architectures. Consequently, neither manycore nor dataflow 
architectures are well-suited for such cases.
In computational systems, when executing a large number of dependent instructions—
where data access is minimal—a multicore processor architecture benefits from higher 
clock frequencies. This configuration allows for execution time that scales nearly linearly 
with the number of instructions. Conversely, a manycore system may remain underuti-
lized if the instructions cannot be effectively parallelized due to interdependencies.

However, if the instructions involve independent iterations of a for-loop, or if the algo-
rithm can be restructured to render these iterations independent, a manycore system can 
achieve significant performance improvements. In such cases, multiple cores can execute 
several for-loop iterations concurrently.
Dataflow architectures are particularly well-suited to accelerate these types of instruc-
tions. In this context, instructions can be implemented on field-programmable gate arrays, 
which facilitate direct data flow between instructions. For instance, in a scenario with 
10,000 instructions within a for-loop, the dataflow hardware’s pipeline will become fully 
populated after 10,000 cycles. Thereafter, the dataflow hardware will produce output con-
tinuously, with each subsequent result emerging at the output on each clock cycle.
Dataflow hardware is specifically engineered for executing repetitive, independent 
instructions with minimal data access requirements. This architecture allows for the effi-
cient pipelining of all instructions within a given iteration. Consequently, once the pipeline 
is fully populated, new outputs can be generated on each successive clock cycle, thereby 
maximizing throughput and reducing latency.
Dataflow hardware is generally optimized for scenarios where algorithms involve repeti-
tive execution of independent instructions with minimal data dependencies. However, for 
big data algorithms that perform fundamental processing on each data element, such hard-
ware may not be ideally suited. Nevertheless, dataflow hardware can still offer performance 
benefits in these contexts by leveraging its parallel data access capabilities. Specifically, the 
hardware’s architecture enables concurrent retrieval of data from dataflow memory, which 
can accelerate the overall processing of large datasets despite the inherent limitations of the 
dataflow model for complex data operations.
In addition to its capability for parallel data access, when there is a relatively high num-
ber of instructions that are repeated, dataflow hardware can implement instructions in a 
pipelined manner, which enhances its suitability for certain algorithms. This pipelining 
capability allows for continuous processing of instructions by structuring them into succes-
sive stages within the hardware. As a result, algorithms that can be decomposed into dis-
crete, sequential processing stages benefit from the efficient execution provided by dataflow 
architectures.
When evaluating the suitability of dataflow hardware for a given algorithm, particu-
larly one that operates on large datasets and exhibits complex, branching processing paths 
dependent on the data, it is essential to consider both the size of the dataflow hardware and 
its capacity to manage the resources required for storing all potential paths. The efficacy 
of dataflow hardware cannot be determined solely based on its general compatibility with 
high-volume data; instead, a comprehensive assessment must account for the hardware’s 
ability to handle the specific demands of the algorithm, including the storage and manage-
ment of all possible computational paths. Even if the dataflow hardware can fit all possible 
paths, there are no guarantees that dataflow hardware will be utilized enough.
Decomposition of high‑performance computing algorithms for control‑flow and dataflow 
architectures
This section outlines the fundamental principles of fine-grain algorithm analysis within 
the context of high-performance computing. The execution of most high-performance 
algorithms can be segmented into the following primary phases:

–	 Data initialization phase
–	 Data processing phase.
Additionally, many algorithms necessitate a final stage of processing before their 
execution concludes. This final stage, termed the Finalizing Phase, may involve aggre-
gating results or performing additional computations to prepare the data for storage, 
presentation, or further analysis. For instance, if an algorithm’s data processing phase 
involves iterative computations over a simulation volume across multiple time steps, 
the results might need aggregation before being written to main memory, files, or pre-
sented to users. This finalizing process is analogous to the data initialization phase.
The Data Processing Phase can be further classified into two distinct categories:
–	 Uniform processing
–	 Processing edge cases.
In control-flow architectures, the distinction between processing inner elements 
and edge elements of a matrix is generally minimal. However, dataflow architectures 
require specific configurations to handle data streaming effectively through the hard-
ware. Although dataflow hardware can process both inner and edge elements, incor-
porating both types of processing within the same kernel can complicate the kernel’s 
design. This complexity can reduce readability, increase the number of required con-
ditionals (and thus hardware require more effort [26]). Additionally, this can slow 
down execution in certain scenarios.

ment of code can run either on control-flow or dataflow hardware), a programmer 
can determine what is the best way to accelerate the algorithm for certain inputs.

The Maxeler framework is designed to enable the simulation of the hardware before

A publicly available dataflow implementation of the Lattice-Boltzmann method is 
designed for dataflow hardware [27]. Algorithm 2 illustrates the implementation of the 
Lattice-Boltzmann stream function in MaxJ language for dataflow hardware. In this 
implementation, corner cases are handled by a separate kernel, effectively isolating the 
computation of edge elements in matrices of dimensions 320 × 112 from the processing 
of inner elements. This separation simplifies the kernel designed for inner elements by 
reducing its complexity.
Similarly, the collide function, which constitutes a significant portion of the total 
execution time, also involves numerous conditional statements. These statements dis-
tinguish between processing edge elements and inner elements of the matrix. The con-
ditional nature of these statements necessitates a control-flow processor to supply the 
kernel with all required data, even when dealing with edge elements where some sur-
rounding data might be absent. The use of conditional statements in a single kernel to 
handle both edge and inner elements would otherwise lead to an impractically large 
number of kernels if separate kernels were created for each edge and corner case. Spe-
cifically, implementing separate kernels for each edge and corner element would require

Empirical evidence shows that the dataflow implementation of the Lattice-Boltzmann

Max2 card was used in conjunction with the latest i5 processor. The observed average

and another for edge and corner elements), a dataflow implementation with a single 
kernel for inner matrix elements utilizes about half of the dataflow hardware resources. 
Given that multicore processors can handle any matrix element and that there are more 
inner elements than edge elements, it is pragmatic to process only inner matrix elements

Acceleration of the Lattice‑Boltzmann method
This study assumes that the kernel processing matrix edges consumes similar dataflow 
resources as the kernel for non-edge matrix elements, notwithstanding the additional 
resources required for conditional statements. The Lattice-Boltzmann method involves 
multiple matrices, with the dataflow implementation processing a total of nine matrices. 
These principles apply consistently across all matrices.
The Maxeler framework’s inability to predict the resource usage of dual kernels at 
compile time implies that the deployment of kernels may lead to underutilization of 
dataflow hardware resources. With an equal number of instances for both kernels, a sub-
stantial portion of dataflow hardware resources may remain idle.
To address this underutilization, it is proposed that edge elements be processed using 
control-flow hardware. This control-flow implementation of the Lattice-Boltzmann 
method operates on matrices of width 320 and height 112. If doubling the number of 
dataflow kernels for inner elements doubles the instruction per second ratio, the theo-
retical acceleration factor is approximately 220 [29, 30].
Given that edge elements can be processed by the multicore processor, it is essential to 
compare the processing times for edge elements on the multicore processor with those 
for inner matrix elements on the dataflow hardware. The multicore processor handles 
two rows of width-1 elements and two rows of height-1 elements, totaling 860 edge ele-
ments. Distributing these across 16 cores results in approximately 54 elements per core. 
Conversely, the dataflow hardware processes height-2 rows of width-2 elements, total-
ing 34,980 inner matrix elements. With an acceleration factor of 220, the dataflow pro-
cessing time equates to processing 159 elements on a single control-flow processor core. 
Therefore, the multicore processor can manage edge elements while exchanging data 
with the dataflow hardware, which processes the remaining matrix elements.

Threats to validity
The method proposed for decomposing control-flow algorithms to enhance execution 
speed and reduce energy consumption is applicable to only a subset of high-perfor-
mance computing algorithms. The reported acceleration factor does not account for the 
increased spatial requirements and transistor count associated with hybrid processors, 
which combine control-flow and dataflow functionalities. Although hybrid processors 
might require more space compared to individual control-flow or dataflow hardware 
components, they potentially offer a net gain in efficiency by integrating the advantages 
of both architectures. Specifically, existing dataflow hardware is often used in conjunc-
tion with control-flow hardware to optimize data manipulation and algorithm initiali-
zation, thereby improving overall performance. Consequently, the space required for a 
hybrid processor may be less than the combined space needed for separate control-flow 
and dataflow components.
Future research should investigate the suitability of the proposed hybrid architecture 
in meeting evolving computational demands. Potential research avenues include decom-
posing algorithms with existing dataflow implementations to evaluate the applicability of 
the proposed method to currently utilized algorithms. Additionally, exploring the paral-
lelization of database queries could provide insights into further accelerating algorithm 
execution.
Conclusions
Dataflow hardware can execute certain high-performance computing algorithms signifi-
cantly faster—by an order of magnitude or more—compared to traditional control-flow 
processors based on the von Neumann architecture. However, due to the inherent con-
straints of dataflow hardware, the execution of most algorithms still relies on control-
flow processors. Often, communication between dataflow and control-flow hardware is 
necessary during algorithm execution. Given the substantial architectural differences, 
these components are typically implemented on separate chips. Recent advancements 
suggest the feasibility of integrating both control-flow and dataflow architectures onto a 
single hybrid chip.
This study focuses on the algorithmic aspects of utilizing hybrid control-flow and 
dataflow architectures. With the ability to transfer data between control-flow and data-
flow components at cache memory speeds, certain high-performance computing algo-
rithms can benefit from executing specific portions on each architecture. For instance, 
the dataflow and control-flow implementation of the Lattice-Boltzmann method dem-
onstrates that the algorithm can be accelerated by approximately a factor of two com-
pared to using dataflow hardware alone.
The proposed approach to algorithm decomposition for parallel execution on both 
control-flow and dataflow architectures is highly optimized. However, it may be neces-
sary to run the control-flow portion of the algorithm in parallel across multiple cores to

programming complexity, requiring a programmer to develop a custom manager, instead 
of the default one provided by the framework, and orchestrate data movement manually.

Nenad Korolija   is with the faculty of the School of Electrical Engineering, University of Belgrade, Serbia. 
He received a PhD degree in electrical engineering and computer science in 2017. His interests and experi-
ences include developing software for high-performance computer architectures and Dataflow architec-
tures. In 2008, he worked on the HIPEAC FP7 project at the University of Siena, Italy. In 2013, he was an

Abstract: The execution time of a high-performance computing algorithm is influenced by vari- ous factors, including the algorithm’s scalability, the selected hardware for processing elements, and the communication speed between these elements. This study utilizes a hybrid architecture that integrates both control-flow and dataflow hardware. Specifi- cally, the control-flow hardware encompasses both multicore and manycore architec- tures. Guidance for dataflow programmers is provided to enable them to anticipate the level of acceleration achievable with a hybrid control-flow and dataflow architec- ture before developing dataflow hardware algorithms. Furthermore, the methodology developed is introduced, offering a structured approach for programmers to decom- pose algorithms and optimize each segment by leveraging the most suitable archi- tectural type. The prerequisite for a programmer is not to know hardware description languages, but he must be well-versed in estimating the complexity of an algorithm. This study represents the culmination of over a decade of expertise in hybrid control- flow and dataflow architectures. It provides a detailed methodology for decomposing a control-flow algorithm into segments optimized for dataflow architectures and those better suited to control-flow architectures. The Lattice-Boltzmann method is employed as a representative example, implemented on both control-flow and dataflow hard- ware. The estimated total acceleration factor of the decomposed Lattice-Boltzmann method on the hybrid architecture, relative to execution times using control-flow and dataflow hardware, is approximately two for a given matrix dimension. The find- ings underscore the advantages of employing a hybrid architecture, demonstrating significant acceleration potential even for algorithms traditionally optimized for data- flow architectures. The primary benefit of the hybrid architecture lies in its capac- ity to accelerate algorithms where only specific portions are suitable for dataflow hardware.
